headline: The US government drops its 13-year case against IBM
text: On 8 January the Justice Department dismissed its antitrust suit against IBM, calling it "without merit". The case was filed in 1969 and had hung over the world's biggest computer maker for almost thirteen years. IBM is no longer threatened with being split up.

headline: AT&T agrees to give up its local phone companies
text: On the same day as the IBM decision, the Justice Department and AT&T announced a settlement of the suit filed against the phone giant in 1974. AT&T will divest the local Bell operating companies. The phone company most Americans know is to be broken up.

headline: Commodore shows a home computer, the Commodore 64
text: Commodore International introduced the Commodore 64 in Las Vegas on 7 January. It is a computer for the home, one more maker joining the personal computer market.

headline: Intel launches the 80286, a chip that can use 16 megabytes of memory
text: On 1 February Intel introduced the 80286 microprocessor, with 134,000 transistors. Its address range reaches 16 megabytes of memory, sixteen times the limit of the 8086 chip it follows. It is the processor, the brain, of a personal computer.

headline: Boeing's new 757 jet makes its first flight
text: The Boeing 757 took off on its first flight on 19 February. Eastern Air Lines and British Airways committed to the plane in 1978, 40 aircraft between them.

headline: Banks charge their best customers 16.5%
text: The prime rate, which banks charge their best borrowers, was raised to 17% on 18 February and trimmed to 16.5% five days later. Loans cost this much because the Federal Reserve, under Paul Volcker, is fighting inflation with very high interest rates. Businesses and home buyers are paying the price.

headline: Laker Airways collapses, stranding 6,000 passengers
text: Britain's cut-price airline Laker Airways collapsed on 5 February owing 270 million pounds, with about 6,000 travellers stranded. It is a sign of how hard times are for airlines.

headline: The Ocean Ranger oil rig sinks off Canada with 84 men aboard
text: The drilling platform Ocean Ranger sank in a storm off Newfoundland on 15 February and all 84 workers died. Waves were up to 20 metres high, and rescuers could not reach the men in the freezing water in time. The rig was working for Mobil.

headline: Buffett: Berkshire's book value per share up to 526.02 dollars
text: In his letter of 26 February Warren Buffett reports operating earnings of 39.7 million dollars for 1981, down from 41.9 million, and book value per share of 526.02 dollars, up from 400.80. Berkshire's 7.2 million GEICO shares are worth 199.8 million dollars, against the 47 million it paid. Its Washington Post stake is worth 58.2 million.

headline: The US bans Libyan oil imports
text: President Reagan's government imposed an embargo on Libyan oil on 10 March. Libya sells oil on the world market, so the ban turns oil into a tool of politics.

headline: Argentines raise their flag on South Georgia, near the Falklands
text: On 19 March Argentine forces raised their national flag on South Georgia, an island Britain rules in the far South Atlantic. Argentina also claims the nearby Falkland Islands.

headline: McDonald's sold 7.1 billion dollars in 1981 and has 6,739 restaurants
text: In its letter of 1 March McDonald's reports that sales of all its restaurants together passed 7 billion dollars in 1981, with 2.5 billion in revenue and 265 million in net income. It opened 476 restaurants in 1981 and has 6,739 in 29 countries. It is testing a chicken sandwich and Chicken McNuggets.

headline: Bankgesellschaft takes over Hyposwiss after a fraud loss
text: Bankgesellschaft already owned 52.7% of Hyposwiss, a small bank in Solothurn, when crooked dealings by its managers caused an 11.2 million franc loss in 1981. Bankgesellschaft offered the other shareholders 460 francs a share. When the offer closed on 15 March it held more than 98%. Bankgesellschaft said the fraud left it no choice but to take over the whole bank.
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 1 April 1982 ('Erfolgreiche Uebernahme der Hyposwiss durch die SBG'), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1982-04-01.pdf (read 2026-10-03)

headline: Argentina invades the Falkland Islands
text: Argentine troops landed near Stanley on 1 April and the British governor, Rex Hunt, surrendered the Falklands on 2 April. South Georgia fell on 3 April. Britain answered by retaking South Georgia on 26 April.

headline: McDonald's opens its first restaurant in Malaysia
text: The first McDonald's in Malaysia opened on 29 April on Jalan Bukit Bintang, a busy street in Kuala Lumpur. The burger chain keeps adding countries even while the world economy is weak.

headline: Israel completes its withdrawal from the Sinai
text: On 25 April Israel finished handing the Sinai peninsula back to Egypt, as the 1979 peace treaty required. Two days earlier soldiers had cleared the town of Yamit, where some settlers barricaded themselves on rooftops, and Ariel Sharon ordered the town demolished. For Israelis it meant giving up land held since 1967 for peace with Egypt.

headline: West Germany's Nicole wins Eurovision with 'A Little Peace'
text: Nicole won the Eurovision Song Contest in Harrogate, England, on 24 April with "Ein bisschen Frieden", which means "a little bit of peace". It is West Germany's first win, and she led the voting from start to finish.

headline: GE lays off appliance workers as house building slumps
text: On 1 April General Electric announced 275 permanent layoffs at Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky, and temporary furloughs for 8,000 more workers from 3 May. Fewer new houses mean fewer refrigerators, ovens and washing machines sold: factory shipments of big appliances were 14.1% lower than a year earlier.

headline: Schweizerische Bankgesellschaft, the Union Bank, is now available to you
text: Bankgesellschaft, called Union Bank of Switzerland abroad, was formed in 1912 when the Bank in Winterthur (1862) and the Toggenburger Bank (1863) merged. It has grown by buying smaller banks and is a leading European underwriter of Eurobonds, bonds sold across borders. It ranks among Switzerland's big three banks.

headline: Schweizerischer Bankverein, the Swiss Bank Corporation, is now available to you
text: The Bankverein began in Basel in 1854, when six private banks pooled their money, and became the Basler Bankverein in 1872. Its assets grew from 4 billion Swiss francs at the end of the 1950s to 74 billion in 1979. It is one of Switzerland's three biggest banks, with a big home network and growing business for companies in the United States.

headline: Schweizerische Kreditanstalt, the Swiss Credit Bank, is now available to you
text: Alfred Escher founded the Kreditanstalt on 5 July 1856 to lend money for railways; it later helped finance the Gotthard line. In 1977 a scandal at its Chiasso branch, where Italian deposits went into risky investments, hurt its name. In 1978 it took a 44% stake in the US firm First Boston.

headline: Exxon cancels its giant shale oil project in Colorado
text: On 2 May Exxon announced it was ending the Colony shale oil project, citing low oil prices and rising costs. It had paid 300 million dollars for a 60% stake in 1980. More than 2,000 workers lost their jobs; locals call the day "Black Sunday".

headline: Britain sinks the General Belgrano; an Exocet sinks HMS Sheffield
text: The Falklands war turned deadly. The British submarine Conqueror sank the Argentine cruiser General Belgrano on 2 May, killing 323 sailors. Two days later an Exocet missile hit HMS Sheffield; 20 died. On 25 May the Atlantic Conveyor and HMS Coventry were lost too.

headline: Iran retakes Khorramshahr from Iraq
text: Iranian troops retook the port city of Khorramshahr from Iraq on 24 May after a month-long offensive. Iran said it captured 15,000 to 19,000 Iraqi soldiers. The victory pushed Iraqi troops out of most of southern Iran and showed that Iran was no longer losing the war.

headline: Europe opens a competition case against Philip Morris over Rothmans
text: On 30 May the European Commission said it had opened a cartel case against Philip Morris. In 1981 Philip Morris paid South Africa's Rembrandt 350 million dollars for half of the holding that controls the British cigarette maker Rothmans International. Three European cigarette makers complained that the deal could give Philip Morris too much power in Europe.
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 1 June 1982 (sda/dpa report, Brussels, 30 May), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1982-06-01.pdf (read 2026-10-03); https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:61984CJ0142 (read 2026-10-03)

headline: Oil-service shares keep sliding; Schlumberger in the low $40s
text: On Wall Street at the end of May, oil-service shares continued their slide: Schlumberger fell to a little over 43 dollars, Halliburton to about 30 and Dresser to 19. Oil shares, the market's favourites last summer, have fallen out of favour; Mesa Petroleum, for example, dropped from 34 dollars last summer to about 12 this spring.
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 29 May 1982 (New York market report), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1982-05-29.pdf (read 2026-10-03); Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 1 June 1982 (Mesa Petroleum), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1982-06-01.pdf (read 2026-10-03)

headline: Coca-Cola buys Columbia Pictures for 750 million dollars
text: The soft drink maker said on 22 June it will buy the Hollywood studio Columbia Pictures for 750 million dollars. Columbia has had hits such as Kramer vs. Kramer, Stripes and The Blue Lagoon. Coca-Cola is betting that movies can grow its business as fast as drinks.

headline: Argentina surrenders in the Falklands
text: Argentine forces surrendered at Stanley on 14 June, ending a war of about ten weeks. The Argentine president, Leopoldo Galtieri, resigned on 18 June. Britain has kept the islands.

headline: Israel invades Lebanon
text: Israeli forces invaded Lebanon on 6 June under Defence Minister Ariel Sharon, with about 60,000 troops and over 800 tanks. The stated aim was to push PLO fighters 40 kilometres north of the border. By the end of the month Israeli troops had reached the edge of Beirut and surrounded PLO and Syrian forces in the west of the city, far beyond that aim.

headline: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial opens in cinemas
text: The science-fiction film E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, directed by Steven Spielberg, was released on 11 June. It cost $10.5 million to make and took $11 million in its opening weekend, finishing number one at the US box office. Critic Roger Ebert gave it four stars out of four.

headline: Coca-Cola launches Diet Coke in New York
text: Diet Coke debuted in New York City on 8 July. It is a sugar-free version of the famous drink, a new product from the company's biggest brand.

headline: Penn Square Bank in Oklahoma fails; big banks are stung
text: Penn Square, a small bank in Oklahoma City, was shut on 5 July with about 525 million dollars in assets. It had made risky oil loans and sold over a billion dollars' worth of shares in them to other banks, including Chicago's Continental Illinois and Seafirst of Seattle.

headline: Banks start cutting the prime rate
text: Banks lowered the prime rate on 20 July to 16% and again on 29 July to 15.5%. These were the first cuts in months, and borrowing is getting cheaper after a year of very high rates.

headline: Disney's TRON opens, a film built on computer graphics
text: Disney's science-fiction film TRON opened on 9 July. It cost about 17 million dollars and is Disney's venture into computer graphics.

headline: Wall Street starts a huge rally
text: After a low of 776.92 on 12 August, the Dow Jones average jumped nearly 39 points on 17 August, its biggest one-day gain ever, as 92.9 million shares traded. The next day, for the first time, more than 100 million shares changed hands. The rally began when Henry Kaufman, a Salomon Brothers economist, said interest rates would fall to single digits within a year.

headline: Mexico says it cannot pay its foreign debts
text: On 12 August Mexico told its lenders it could no longer pay its foreign debt and asked for a 90-day pause. It had borrowed heavily in dollars against its oil income, and the oil price has fallen. Banks around the world will have to rethink lending to poorer countries.

headline: The prime rate falls to 14%
text: On 18 August banks cut the prime rate to 14%. It was 16.5% in February and 15.5% at the end of July.

headline: Boeing delivers its first 767 to United Airlines
text: Boeing handed over the first 767 airliner to United Airlines on 19 August, after it was certified on 30 July. When the first one was shown in August 1981, Boeing already had 173 firm orders from 17 airlines.

headline: The first compact discs are pressed in Germany
text: The first compact discs for music were made at a plant in Germany on 17 August. Music on a disc instead of vinyl or tape is a new idea.

headline: Wal-Mart's founder makes the first Forbes 400 list
text: Forbes magazine published its first list of the 400 richest Americans. Oil and shipping owner Daniel Ludwig came first with 2 billion dollars, and Wal-Mart founder Sam Walton is on the list too. You needed 75 million dollars just to get on it.

headline: The Boeing 767 enters passenger service
text: United Airlines flew the first passengers on a Boeing 767 on 8 September. It is the first of Boeing's new generation of jets to carry customers.

headline: Cyanide-laced Tylenol capsules kill seven in Chicago
text: Seven people in the Chicago area died on 28 and 29 September after taking Tylenol capsules, made by Johnson & Johnson, that someone had filled with potassium cyanide. The victims included a 12-year-old girl and three members of one family. Tests found the capsules came from two different factories, so the poison must have been added after the bottles reached the shops, and police warned everyone not to take Tylenol.

headline: Lebanon's president-elect is assassinated
text: Bachir Gemayel, the Lebanese president-elect, was killed by a bomb in Beirut on 14 September. On 18 September a massacre of Palestinians took place in the Sabra and Shatila camps.

headline: Disney opens EPCOT Center in Florida
text: EPCOT Center opened at Walt Disney World on 1 October, after an investment of more than a billion dollars. It is a big bet for Disney in a year of recession.

headline: Sony starts selling the world's first CD player
text: The Sony CDP-101, the first commercially available compact disc player, went on sale on 1 October. It plays the new compact discs.

headline: Helmut Kohl becomes West Germany's Chancellor
text: Helmut Kohl of the Christian Democrats became West Germany's chancellor on 1 October, after the small Free Democratic party left Helmut Schmidt's government and voted with Kohl to remove him. It is the first time a chancellor has been replaced by such a vote.

headline: The prime rate drops to 12% and savings banks are freed
text: Banks cut the prime rate to 13% on 7 October and 12% on 13 October. On 15 October the Garn-St Germain Act deregulated savings and loan institutions.

headline: Henry VIII's warship the Mary Rose is lifted from the sea
text: The Mary Rose, King Henry VIII's flagship, was raised from the Solent on 11 October. She sank in 1545.

headline: The Dow shoots to 1,065 on record volume
text: The Dow Jones average rose 43.41 points to 1,065.49 on 3 November. Trading volume on the New York Stock Exchange hit a record 149.4 million shares on 4 November. Shares are rising on hopes that lower interest rates will end the recession.

headline: Andropov takes over from Brezhnev in Moscow
text: Yuri Andropov was chosen on 12 November, two days after Leonid Brezhnev died, to lead the Soviet Communist Party as general secretary. He was 68 and the first former head of the KGB to take the job. Western newspapers greeted him with unease, because his own background was largely unknown to them.

headline: BMW shows the new 3 Series
text: BMW released the second generation of its 3 Series, the compact model, at the end of November 1982. It was the first 3 Series offered as a four-door saloon and as an estate, and its suspension was revised to curb the tail-sliding that critics had disliked in the old car. Buyers now got a small BMW that suited a family.

headline: Michael Jackson releases Thriller
text: Michael Jackson put out his new album Thriller at the end of November, produced by Quincy Jones. It was recorded in seven months at a cost of $750,000 and includes "Beat It" and "Billie Jean" as well as a duet with Paul McCartney. Release was brought forward from January after copies leaked to radio stations.

headline: The Vietnam Veterans Memorial is dedicated in Washington
text: The black granite wall carrying the names of the American dead of the Vietnam War was dedicated on 13 November, at the end of a five-day salute to Vietnam veterans. It carries 57,939 names. The design by the young architect Maya Lin had been attacked by critics as "a black gash of shame and sorrow", but for many veterans and families it became a place to find a name.

headline: French consumer group calls for a boycott of Nestle
text: On 30 November the French consumer union UFC called on shoppers to boycott Nestle products, to force a change in how Nestle sells baby milk in poor countries. Nestle said it was surprised, since it is the only baby-milk maker that has promised to follow the World Health Organization's code. The two sides will meet in Paris.
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 1 December 1982 ('Nestle und der WHO-Kodex', sda, Bern, 30 November), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1982-12-01.pdf (read 2026-10-03)

headline: Unemployment is at 10.8%, the worst since the 1930s
text: The US unemployment rate reached 10.8% in November, the highest since the Great Depression. Interest rates are falling now that the Federal Reserve has eased its policy, but jobs are still scarce; in Michigan the rate hit 14.5% in September.

headline: The Dow ends 1982 at 1,046.54, up 19.6%
text: Shares had their best year in seven years: the Dow gained 171.54 points, or 19.6%, closing at 1,046.54. Since the August low of 776.92 it is up 37.7%. A record 16.46 billion shares changed hands.

headline: IBM pays 250 million dollars for 12% of Intel
text: IBM agreed on 22 December to buy 12% of Intel's shares for 250 million dollars, and could go up to 30%. Intel makes the chips in IBM's personal computers, and the cash helps it through the recession. IBM paid 40 dollars a share.

headline: Mercedes-Benz presents the 190, its smallest car
text: Daimler-Benz presented the Mercedes 190 on 8 December. It is the company's first compact car, developed since 1974.

headline: The Boeing 757 is certified and delivered to Eastern
text: The 757 won US certification on 21 December and Eastern Air Lines took delivery of the first one on 22 December. It is a twin-engine jet for about 200 passengers on short and medium routes, built to replace the Boeing 727. Eastern and British Airways had placed the first orders in 1978, and the plane first flew in February 1982.

headline: Wal-Mart moves into Florida and Nebraska
text: Through 1982 Wal-Mart kept pushing out of its Southern home region, with its first stores in Florida and Nebraska. Sam Walton's discount chain is growing state by state.

headline: Time magazine names the personal computer Machine of the Year
text: At the end of December Time magazine named the personal computer its Machine of the Year, instead of choosing a person. IBM's PC, launched less than two years ago, has sold far beyond what IBM expected.
